title: Spring: @Transactional, rollback rules and JdbcTemplate
description: Spring @Transactional propagation, rollback rules and the self-invocation trap; readOnly, isolation defaults, JdbcTemplate and parameter binding.
source: Spring Framework documentation (transaction management, declarative rollback, JdbcTemplate and NamedParameterJdbcTemplate); Hibernate ORM user guide (flush modes); PostgreSQL documentation (transaction isolation); Baeldung
seriesTitle: Interview roadmap: Java and Spring Boot
seriesDescription: Java and Spring Boot interview topics in JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short Java/SQL code and multi-correct questions. Java only: nothing here mixes in Python.

questions.prompt: Match each Spring transaction propagation to its behaviour.

right.text: Joins the caller's transaction, or starts one if none exists
Suspends the caller's transaction and runs in a new, independent one
Joins a transaction if present, otherwise runs non-transactionally
Throws if there is no existing transaction
Throws if a transaction already exists
Runs inside a savepoint of the current transaction (JDBC)
Always joins the parent and ignores the method's own rollback rules

questions.explanation: REQUIRES_NEW commits or rolls back independently of the caller (it needs a second connection, so it can deadlock a tiny pool). NESTED uses savepoints and works only with JDBC-style transaction managers.

questions.prompt: In one Spring bean (default proxy-based AOP), @Transactional public void place() calls this.audit(), which is annotated @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW). A controller calls place() on the injected bean. How many physical database transactions are started?
questions.explanation: The call this.audit() never passes through the Spring proxy, so the REQUIRES_NEW advice is not applied and audit() simply runs inside place()'s transaction. Move audit() to another bean (or use AspectJ mode) to get the second transaction.

questions.prompt: OrderService.place() is @Transactional (REQUIRED). It inserts row A, then calls auditBean.log(), a method of a different bean annotated REQUIRES_NEW, which inserts row B and throws a RuntimeException. place() catches that exception, inserts row C and returns normally. How many of the rows A, B, C are committed?
questions.explanation: B belongs to its own transaction, which rolled back; the outer transaction is unaffected, so A and C commit. If log() were REQUIRED instead, the shared transaction would be marked rollback-only and the outer commit would throw UnexpectedRollbackException, leaving 0 rows.

questions.prompt: OrderService.place() is @Transactional (REQUIRED). It inserts row A, then calls a method of another bean that is also REQUIRED, inserts row B and throws a RuntimeException. place() catches that exception, inserts row C and returns normally. How many of the rows A, B, C are committed?
questions.explanation: The inner REQUIRED method joined the same transaction, and its RuntimeException crossed the proxy and marked the transaction rollback-only. When place() finishes, the commit fails with UnexpectedRollbackException and nothing is committed.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: A @Transactional method called through this.method() from another method of the same class does not get the intended transactional behaviour under default proxy mode.
questions.reason: Spring applies transactions through a proxy wrapped around the bean, and a call on this does not pass through that proxy.

whys.a: Correct: the proxy is the only place where begin/commit/rollback advice runs, and this bypasses it.
whys.b: R is the actual cause, so it is the correct explanation.
whys.c: R is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.
whys.d: A is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.

questions.explanation: The same proxy limitation applies to @Async, @Cacheable and @Retryable. Fixes: call through another bean, inject the proxy of yourself, restructure, or use AspectJ weaving.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: A checked exception such as IOException thrown out of a @Transactional method rolls the transaction back by default.
questions.reason: Spring's default rollback rule applies to RuntimeException and Error only.

whys.a: A is false, so both-true options are wrong.
whys.b: A is false, so both-true options are wrong.
whys.c: R is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.
whys.d: Correct: the default is commit on checked exceptions; use rollbackFor = Exception.class to change it.

questions.explanation: This mirrors EJB semantics (checked exceptions are business exceptions). Interviewers love this trap: a method throwing IOException after a debit still commits unless rollbackFor is set.

questions.prompt: Complete the rules by dragging the right words into the blanks.
questions.text: Add {1} = Exception.class to roll back on checked exceptions. Propagation.{2} suspends the caller's transaction and starts a new one. A call made through {3} bypasses the Spring proxy, so no transaction logic is applied. If an inner REQUIRED method throws and the caller swallows it, the shared transaction is already marked {4}.
questions.explanation: The rollback-only flag is why the outer commit fails with UnexpectedRollbackException even though the caller caught the exception.

questions.prompt: Annotate the service method `void audit(String msg) throws IOException` so that it always runs in its own new transaction and also rolls back when the checked IOException is thrown.

checks.label: requests a new transaction with REQUIRES_NEW
rolls back for checked exceptions via rollbackFor

questions.model:
@Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW, rollbackFor = Exception.class)
void audit(String msg) throws IOException { /* ... */ }
questions.explanation: rollbackFor = IOException.class is also fine. Remember the annotation only takes effect when audit() is invoked from another bean through the proxy.

questions.prompt: A NamedParameterJdbcTemplate called `named` and a String variable `status` exist. Write the call that returns, as an Integer, the number of rows in table orders whose status column equals that variable, binding it as the named parameter :status.

checks.label: passes a parameter map or source

questions.explanation: new MapSqlParameterSource("status", status) works too. Never concatenate the value into the SQL string.

questions.prompt: With a JdbcTemplate called jdbc, int qty and long id, write the statement that decrements products.stock by qty for that product only if stock is at least qty, binding values with ? placeholders, and keeps the number of affected rows in int rows.
questions.explanation: rows == 0 means the guard failed (not enough stock or no such product), so the caller reports a conflict. A single guarded UPDATE is atomic and needs no explicit locking.

questions.prompt: Select all true statements about Spring JdbcTemplate.

options.text: queryForObject throws EmptyResultDataAccessException when no row matches.
options.why: Right: it never returns null for a missing row.

options.text: update(...) returns the number of rows affected.
options.why: Right: useful for optimistic checks (0 means nothing matched).

options.text: It translates SQLException into the unchecked DataAccessException hierarchy.
options.why: Right: callers do not handle checked SQLExceptions.

options.text: It keeps a first-level cache of query results like Hibernate.
options.why: JdbcTemplate is stateless and caches nothing.

options.text: queryForObject returns null when no row matches.
options.why: It throws instead; use query(...) and check the list for an optional result.

questions.explanation: JdbcTemplate removes connection/statement/exception boilerplate but stays plain SQL: you map rows yourself with RowMapper and manage the SQL.

questions.prompt: Which JdbcTemplate call is safe against SQL injection?

options.text: jdbc.queryForList("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?", name)
options.why: Correct: the value is bound as a parameter, never parsed as SQL.

options.text: jdbc.queryForList("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'")
options.why: String concatenation lets a quote in the value rewrite the statement.

options.text: jdbc.queryForList(String.format("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '%s'", name))
options.why: String.format is still concatenation and equally injectable.

options.text: jdbc.queryForList("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?" + name)
options.why: It appends the value to the SQL text and leaves the placeholder unbound.

questions.explanation: Never build SQL from input. Placeholders cannot stand in for identifiers such as column names or ORDER BY direction, so allow-list those.

questions.prompt: True or false: with JPA and Hibernate, a change made to a managed entity inside a @Transactional(readOnly = true) method is still flushed to the database at commit, just like in a normal transaction.

options.why: Wrong: readOnly = true sets the Hibernate session to manual flush mode, so the change is not written.
Correct: readOnly = true puts Hibernate in MANUAL flush mode, so dirty changes are not flushed.

questions.explanation: readOnly = true is a hint that lets Spring set the flush mode to MANUAL and tell the JDBC driver the transaction is read-only. It also saves dirty-checking work on large result sets. It is not a security control: use database privileges for that.

questions.prompt: True or false: a RuntimeException that leaves a @Transactional method (called through the proxy) marks the transaction for rollback by default.

options.why: Correct: unchecked exceptions and errors trigger rollback with no extra configuration.
Wrong: Spring's default rollback rule does cover RuntimeException and Error.

questions.explanation: Checked exceptions commit by default, which is why rollbackFor = Exception.class is a common setting.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: JdbcTemplate converts SQLException into Spring's unchecked DataAccessException hierarchy.
questions.reason: JdbcTemplate keeps a cache of query results between calls.

whys.a: Wrong: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Correct: A is true (callers handle DuplicateKeyException and friends instead of vendor error codes); R is false because JdbcTemplate is stateless.

questions.explanation: The translation gives portable, unchecked exceptions such as DuplicateKeyException and DataIntegrityViolationException.

questions.prompt: A Spring service uses @Transactional with the default isolation (Isolation.DEFAULT) against PostgreSQL. Which isolation level does each transaction run at?

options.why: Correct: DEFAULT means the database default, and for PostgreSQL that is READ COMMITTED.

options.text: REPEATABLE READ, as in every SQL database.
options.why: REPEATABLE READ is the default of MySQL InnoDB, not of PostgreSQL.

options.text: SERIALIZABLE, because Spring prefers the safest level.
options.why: Spring never upgrades the level on its own; SERIALIZABLE must be requested explicitly.

options.text: READ UNCOMMITTED, to give the best throughput by default.
options.why: PostgreSQL treats READ UNCOMMITTED as READ COMMITTED and Spring does not request it by default.

questions.explanation: Isolation.DEFAULT delegates to the database: READ COMMITTED on PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server, REPEATABLE READ on MySQL InnoDB. Higher levels can raise serialization failures that the application must retry.
